overview: A 2D LiDAR like the RPLIDAR spins one laser in a flat circle, producing a single 360-degree slice through the world. A 3D LiDAR spins a whole vertical stack of laser/detector channels instead of just one — commonly 16, 32, or 64 of them, each fixed at a slightly different vertical angle — so every rotation sweeps out a full 3D point cloud rather than one flat plane. That's what lets a self-driving car or outdoor robot tell the difference between a curb, an overhanging branch, and a person, none of which a flat 2D scan plane can distinguish. The tradeoff is real: it needs a proper power supply (not USB), a Gigabit Ethernet link to move hundreds of thousands of points per second, and a genuinely powerful onboard computer to do anything useful with the resulting data volume.
simpleSummary: A spinning sensor with a whole stack of lasers instead of just one, building a full 3D map instead of a flat 2D scan.

specifications.channels: 16 laser channels (typical entry-level 3D LiDAR channel count)
specifications.interface: Gigabit Ethernet (UDP point cloud stream) + separate power/GPS interconnect

pinMap.name: Power+
pinMap.function: DC power input to the spinning head's motor and internal electronics.
pinMap.voltageRange: 9-32V DC (wide input typical of automotive/industrial LiDAR)
pinMap.gotcha: Current draw spikes noticeably at spin-up as the motor overcomes static friction to reach target RPM — a supply sized only for steady-state draw can brown out on startup.

pinMap.name: Ethernet
pinMap.function: Streams the raw point cloud as UDP packets over 100Base-T/Gigabit Ethernet to the host computer.
pinMap.gotcha: The data rate is high enough that a flaky switch, a WiFi-to-Ethernet bridge, or a cheap unmanaged hub can silently drop UDP packets, showing up as visible gaps or missing sectors in the point cloud rather than an obvious error.

pinMap.name: GPS/PPS Sync
pinMap.function: Optional GPS input used to precisely timestamp each rotation (via the PPS pulse) for synchronizing multiple sensors or georeferencing outdoor scans.
pinMap.gotcha: Leaving this unconnected still works for a single sensor, but a rig combining this LiDAR with a second LiDAR or a camera will accumulate subtle frame-to-frame timing drift without it, corrupting sensor fusion.

useCases.title: Autonomous ground vehicle 3D SLAM
useCases.scenario: Build and localize within a full 3D map of an outdoor environment, distinguishing curbs, overhangs, and obstacles a flat 2D scan would miss entirely.

useCases.title: Off-road/agricultural terrain mapping
useCases.scenario: Sweep a field or job site to build an elevation and vegetation-density map from the 3D point cloud.

useCases.title: Drone 3D obstacle avoidance
useCases.scenario: Detect obstacles above and below the flight plane (wires, branches, overhangs) that a single horizontal scan plane can't see.

useCases.title: Multi-sensor object detection/classification
useCases.scenario: Fuse the point cloud with camera imagery to classify detected objects (pedestrian, vehicle, cyclist) for path planning.

useCases.title: As-built facility 3D scanning
useCases.scenario: Static or slow-moving sweep to capture a warehouse or construction site as a georeferenced 3D point cloud.

oftenConfusedWith: RPLIDAR (spins a single laser in one flat plane, giving a 2D scan; this sensor spins a whole vertical stack of lasers, giving a full 3D point cloud every rotation)

Intel RealSense D435i (a depth camera has a narrow ~90° forward-facing view and ~10m range using stereo image matching; this sees the full 360° around the vehicle out to 100m+ using direct laser time-of-flight)
oftenUpgradedTo: Solid-state/MEMS LiDAR (no spinning parts, higher long-term reliability, narrower FOV per unit but no mechanical wear)

beginnerMistakes: Sizing the power supply for steady-state draw only, missing the startup current spike as the head spins up.
Mounting height/tilt miscalculated so the near-field scan clips the ground plane, flooding the point cloud with 'ground' returns.
Not filtering ground-plane points out before obstacle detection, causing normal floor/road texture to register as false obstacles.
Running the data link over a WiFi bridge instead of direct Ethernet, dropping packets under load.
Underestimating the raw data volume — logging or processing 300,000 points/sec naively can overwhelm a modest onboard computer.
